query: Modelos estadísticos y técnicas de descomposición de señales para estimación y pronóstico de irradiancia solar Analizar modelos estadísticos tradicionales y técnicas de descomposición de señales (EMD, CEEMDAN, VMD) y su integración con modelos de inteligencia artificial para mejorar la precisión del pronóstico. Los modelos estadísticos aportan bases sólidas para el pronóstico, pero presentan limitaciones en capturar dinámicas no lineales y complejas de la irradiancia solar. Las técnicas de descomposición de señales permiten descomponer series temporales complejas en componentes más simples, facilitando la modelación y mejorando la precisión. La integración de descomposición con modelos de deep learning y machine learning híbridos ha demostrado mejoras significativas en la predicción multi-step y en diferentes condiciones estacionales y geográficas. Estos enfoques híbridos requieren cuidadosa selección de variables y preprocesamiento para maximizar su efectividad. Descripción de modelos estadísticos y técnicas de descomposición. Resultados comparativos con modelos tradicionales y de inteligencia artificial. Aplicaciones prácticas en plantas termosolares y regiones con limitaciones de datos. Limitaciones y desafíos en la integración de métodos.

For the benchmarking models, the inputs are determined by the optimum lags. For the GHA station, the inputs comprise 5 previous DNI components, whereas for the TAM sta­ tion, there are 7 previous DNI components. The CAR and CNR stations both utilize 5 previous DNI components. In hybrid models, the number of inputs is determined by the decomposed IMF components from both VMD and SWD, multiplied by the optimum lags. Some of these approaches take into account the influence of atmospheric conditions, particularly aerosols, on Direct Normal Irradiation (DNI) and the efficiency of solar tower plants [4]. Other methods employ advanced computational techniques such as machine learning algorithms [5], deep learning models [6], and hybrid models [7] as robust techniques for DNI forecasting. Each approach has its strengths and limitations, and the choice of method depends on the specific requirements of the application. Traditional methods for direct solar radiation forecasting rely on mathematical models that use meteorological data [8], and physical relationships, expressed as mathematical equations derived from fundamental physical laws (i.e., solar altitude angle, azimuth, clearness index, and turbidity), are key components of these models used for forecasting solar radiation. However, these methods have limitations, particularly in terms of the availability and quality of solar radiation measurement, climatological data, and other atmospheric parameters.

In Figs. 8-11, we present a comparison between the forecasted output of four machine learning models (LS-SVM, GPR, RFR, and ELM) and the corresponding measured DNI in four studied areas, as well as the developed hybrid models. According to our findings, machine-learning models (LS-SVM, GPR, RFR, and ELM) were unable to effectively capture the fluctuations of the DNI time series data, particularly in extreme weather conditions, espe­ cially on cloudy days. This shortcoming can be attributed to their inherent limitations in processing complex patterns and rapid variations in solar irradiance, which are common in such meteorological condi­ tions.
